item.title: Submissions (Issue 0)
item.description:
Submissions


All submissions that are within scope will undergo initial review by the Editorial Board (EB) who collectively vote on whether they will be sent to review. Submissions that fall outside of the journal’s scope may be rejected. Based on the type of work, submissions going to review will then proceed to the corresponding review process.


All submissions should follow our style guide.



Peer-reviewed articles process:

  • Authors should aim for a text that is 3,000-8,000 words in length, although exceptions will be considered
  • Authors should submit an abstract of 150-200 words
  • Submissions will undergo one round of open review by a member of the EB (i.e., the identities of the author and EB member will be known to each other)
  • A second round of anonymous peer review by an outside reviewer
  • Our next Call for Papers will likely be in early 2027. You are welcome to submit through our submissions portal in the meantime, https://academicworks.cuny.edu/hml/, but papers will not be reviewed until the CFP closes.

Non peer-reviewed submission process:

  • Examples include: Creative non-fiction, interviews, personal narratives
  • Creative works should be a maximum of 5,000 words in length, although exceptions will be considered
  • Submissions will undergo review by the Creative Writing Editor or another member of EB
  • Please email non-peer reviewed submissions to inquiries@humanitiesmethods.org. Include your name, institution and contact information with your submission.

Non peer-reviewed book reviews submission process:

  • HML seeks book review submissions that apply humanities methodologies to review both contemporary fiction across genres and nonfiction monographs. Multivolume reference works, scholarly websites, AI platforms, and academic databases are not sought for review at this time. When submitting a proposal, please identify a methodological and/or theoretical approach to help ground the writing as a critical review. These reviews are not purchase recommendations, but rather scholarly analyses of modern texts within our current social, cultural, and political landscape.
  • Maximum 1,500 words in length
  • Submissions will undergo review by Book Review Editor
  • Please email book review submissions to inquiries@humanitiesmethods.org. Include your name, institution and contact information with your submission.


Reviewers will generally make recommendations to authors to improve their submissions. Authors whose papers receive a positive review will be given the opportunity to make revisions and to respond to reviewer feedback. Decisions/review feedback will be communicated to authors by the Managing Editor or Editor in Chief.

Outcomes of review:

  • Accepted
  • Minor revisions required
  • Major revisions required
  • Reject

The Editorial Board will make the final decision whether to publish the submission.

item.title: Editorial, Issue 0 (Issue 0)
item.description:
Editorial


The scholarship of librarianship has long been disproportionately approached from the methodologies and perspectives of the social sciences. We’ve had peer reviewers tell us, without an inkling of self-doubt, that librarianship unambiguously is a social science. But any critically-minded librarian might start asking some pointed questions: Why is this the case? Whose interests does it serve? Who or what is being excluded from these conversations, and for what reasons?


Asking humanistic questions in librarianship is important, not because we are librarians, but because we are human. Yet the intent of this journal is not to revive a faded humanism; rather, we are interested in the contemporary, salient concerns of the discipline. The humanities are not peripheral to the tasks of librarianship, but, when approached with the right tools, very frequently touch upon the exposed nerve of what makes libraries tick today.


Looking at librarianship through this lens will allow us to ask underexplored questions. Humanities approaches offer a huge range of theoretical and methodological strategies to draw upon. Many of us have an educational background in these areas. We know how to do this work. We can constructively broaden and deepen the concerns of librarianship by reconsidering the boundaries of our scholarship.


What’s most amazing to us is that, to our knowledge, other library journals today are not doing this work systematically. At present, librarians writing with humanistic methods are limited to submitting their work to a drastically curtailed set of journals. Alternately, they can shoehorn their work into a social sciences framework to make it publishable as a peer reviewed library paper. This is not a good situation. That such a huge swath of methodological choices is being excluded from our supposedly “interdisciplinary” field is a sign of a systematic failing of our discipline. We can do better.


The incoming editors of this journal have expressed their reasons for participating in this project very clearly. Some have shared statements; we have included them in their entirety. While they speak to broadening the scope of the literature of librarianship -- “through the use of humanities methodologies, we can offer scholarship beyond the ‘usual suspects’ of information literacy, bibliographic instruction, metadata, and cataloging” -- they are also specifically interested in the very human concerns of librarianship: “In a data-driven society that elevates the values of practicality, efficiency, and measurable outcomes, perspectives from the humanities offer insight into the deeper values that underlie the profession.”


As a result, our project is very personal for many of us who want to (or have to) publish in librarianship: “a publication that is open and welcoming of not-strictly-LIS subject matter and approaches is very exciting to someone [...] who may have deep interests that lie at the boundaries of LIS.” Many of us have “witnessed the challenges faced by [colleagues] applying arts-based research methods to librarianship.” While “there is a lack of a reliable publishing venue” for this type of work, thankfully we can change this. We are now starting to do this work; Humanities Methods in Librarianship looks forward to taking on this ambitious and necessary project, with all of you as our collaborators.

by Mark Eaton and the Editorial Board

item.title: Peer Reviewers (Issue 0)
item.description:
Want to become a peer reviewer for Humanities Methods in Librarianship?

If you would like to join our peer reviewer team, please fill out this registration form.

Guidelines for peer reviewers:

  • Peer reviewers must omit any references to themselves. Editors will make the review available to the author(s). Your identity will be hidden. (HML subject editors will not be anonymous; therefore, they do not need to omit references to themselves.)
  • When adding comments or track changes to a submitted paper, please keep the original file format (DOCX or ODT). Track changes functionality only works with DOCX and ODT files. Changing the file format may remove track changes. If you have questions about this, please email inquiries@humanitiesmethods.org.
  • Please make your comments constructive and helpful.
  • You will have an option to upload a cover letter for the Editors only.
  • HML editors and peer reviewers are expected not to use AI tools in the peer review process.

Please consider the following criteria in your review:

  • Originality: Does the paper contain new and significant ideas adequate to justify publication?
  • Relationship to Literature: Does the paper demonstrate an adequate understanding of the relevant literature and cite an appropriate range of sources from the humanities and librarianship? Is any significant work ignored?
  • Argument: Is the paper's argument built on appropriate humanities theory or concepts? Is the research based on clear, well-elaborated arguments? Are the methods employed appropriate for the journal?
  • Conclusions: Are the conclusions presented clearly and appropriately analyzed and communicated? Do the conclusions adequately tie together the arguments of the paper?
  • Quality of Communication: Does the paper clearly express its case, measured against the standards of the field(s) and the expected knowledge of the journal's readership? Has attention been paid to the clarity of expression and readability, such as sentence structure, jargon use, etc.
  • References and Style Guide: Does the paper cite references and generally adhere to formatting guidelines in Chicago Style, 18th edition (Notes and Bibliography)? Is a bibliography included? Can references be verified by finding them in a reputable bibliographic database?

Copyright and Licensing

(Adapted from the Journal of Graduate Librarianship)


Articles, creative works, and book reviews published in Humanities Methods in Librarianship will be licensed with a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0).

Other materials from the Humanities Methods in Librarianship website are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)

Authors retain all copyrights to their works but grant Humanities Methods in Librarianship first publication rights to works accepted for publication.

Retractions

(Adapted from the Journal of Graduate Librarianship)


Correction: Despite the best of efforts, errors occur, and their timely and effective remedy are considered the mark of responsible authors and editors. HML will issue a correction if the scholarly record is seriously affected by errors in a work (e.g., if accuracy/intended meaning, author reputation, or journal reputation is judged to be compromised). HML will not issue a correction for errors that do not affect the work in a material way or significantly alter the reader’s understanding of the work (e.g., misspellings, grammatical errors); the pre-publication review of article proofs is the final opportunity to correct such errors. When a correction is issued, it will link to the published article and also be added to the published article. All corrections will be as concise as possible.

Retraction: HML reserves the right to retract articles, with a retraction defined as a public disavowal, not an erasure or removal. A retraction will occur if the editors and editorial board find that the integrity of the article is undermined due to errors or infringements of research ethics. Retractions could also occur due to undisclosed conflicts of interest or compromised peer review.

Removal: Some circumstances may necessitate removal of an article from HML. This will occur when the article is judged by the editors and editorial board to be defamatory, if it infringes on legal rights, or if there is a reasonable expectation that it will be subject to a court order. The bibliographic information about the article will be retained online, but the article will no longer be available through HML. A note will be added to indicate that the item was removed for legal reasons.

AI Policy

The humanities come to us from the Latin phrase studia humanitatis, which means, quite simply, “education that cultivates a human.” As a humanities-oriented publication, we are uniquely concerned with the ways in which the proponents of generative AI actively seek to undermine humanity—whether through replacing human intellectual labor or through contributing to the continued destruction of the planet.

Given our concerns, we will not publish articles in which AI has been used in either the conceptual (brainstorming, outlining, reading, analyzing, etc.) or productive (writing, revising, editing, etc.) phases of the writing process.

There are some instances in which AI may be used. Accuracy must be verified by the author. Acceptable uses include:

  • Formatting references and in-text citations using bibliographic citation managers
  • Enhancing accessibility
  • Basic spell check and grammar check

HML editors and peer reviewers are expected not to use AI tools in the peer review process.

Papers found to be in violation of this policy will be rejected or retracted. This policy may be revised in the future.

Competing Interests & Recusal Policy

(Adapted from the Journal of Graduate Librarianship and Journal of Librarianship and Scholarly Communication)


All authors of a manuscript are required to declare any competing interests—i.e., past, present or foreseeable future personal, professional, or financial relationships that may have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived by others as having influenced, the information or arguments being presented. Authors should declare their competing interests at the end of their manuscript before the reference list.

All editors and peer reviewers of a manuscript must declare all competing interests and recuse themselves as appropriate from the review and/or decision-making process. Editors and peer reviewers must email the Editor in Chief regarding any competing interests as early as possible. Competing interests will be made known to the Editorial Board and will be communicated in the published version.

Name Change Policy

(Adapted from the Journal of Librarianship and Scholarly Communication)


As part of our commitment to authors and the research community, HML will honor name and pronoun change requests from our authors. This includes, but is not limited to, name changes because of marriage, divorce, gender affirmation, and religious conversion. HML will not require any form of proof or supporting documentation beyond what is needed to confirm the author’s identity and will only note that a non-substantive change was made to the published article.

HML can only make changes to the article (including all of its formats on the HML website) and journal webpage. HML cannot make updates to copies that have already been downloaded, nor can we make changes in indexes/databases that have picked up the original metadata, nor are we able to update citations to articles in which a name change has occurred. HML will not notify co-authors of the change to the article; authors may choose whether or not they wish to alert their co-authors.

Any misuse of this policy will be considered misconduct, and HML reserves the right to investigate and act against misuse.

How to request a name change: Authors who wish to change their name on any work previously published in HML are asked to email the editors.

item.title: Editor Statements, Issue 0 (Issue 0)
item.description:
Editors’ Statements


Vanessa Arce, City University of New York


Despite Library and Information Science (LIS) being an interdisciplinary field, a quick glance at any number of LIS research methods textbooks (including the one used in my Research Methods course in my MLS program) will show that research design methodologies associated with social science research are considered the norm. With the exception of historical research methods, other methodologies associated with disciplines within the Humanities are rarely mentioned in LIS research methods textbooks and courses.

I have made similar observations during my time as a tenure-track library faculty member with publication expectations. Most of the literature in the field I have encountered also draws from social science research methods and thus, despite having a background in the Humanities, my own research is more social science based. I also witnessed the challenges faced by a colleague applying arts-based research methods to librarianship, whose publications were often delayed because journals did not have reviewers in their pool qualified to evaluate articles using this type of methodology in librarianship.

For these reasons, I think it is important to provide a dedicated publication venue for librarian-scholars who want to pursue research using Humanities methodologies. Admittedly, I also have somewhat selfish reasons to participate in this project; I hope that the experience of serving as a co-editor for this journal will inspire me to integrate my literary studies background into my own research in the future.


Johnnie Blunt, University of Northern Iowa


According to a 2017 ALA demographics study, 86.7% of ALA members are White. 4.6% are Black/African American. If these numbers reflect the profession as a whole, librarianship is a predominately White endeavor that represents the cultural norms of a White middle-class population. As one of the few African American men in the profession and one of the small number of librarians with a PhD, I represent the crucial margin that can help evolve and sustain the profession and its scholarly and professional literature.

Librarianship is a different profession for those whose ancestors were routinely forbidden access to education and information. For me and for others like me, librarianship is not simply or largely about organizing knowledge. As a subsection of a larger dominant culture, librarianship is the site of social, cultural, and political tensions. Within this context, information is not equivalent to data; it is the process of humans and events being informed/shaped by various technical and sociopolitical mechanisms that are usually not discussed in the scholarly literature of librarianship.

I joined the editorial board because I believe that HML has the potential to go beyond studies that focus on the technical aspects of librarianships. Through the use of humanities methodologies, we can offer scholarship beyond the "usual suspects" of information literacy, bibliographic instruction, metadata, and cataloging. I want to contribute to social and political discussions of librarianship. Equally important, I want to help marginalized librarians find a place where their voices are heard and respected.


Taylor Pecktal, Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art


I wanted to be a part of HML because getting to contribute to and be a part of a new, open access journal in librarianship is so refreshing to me. I believe that scholarship can and should be accessible to wide audiences, and I’m excited about what this journal will contribute to the field.


Jason Reuscher, Pennsylvania State University


Nearly a quarter century into the new millennium, there is no lack of examples or connections between humanities methods and librarianship. If anything, there is a lack of a reliable publishing venue, and I am both happy and proud to say that this is no longer the case with the creation of Humanities Methods in Librarianship.


Collin Joseph Stevenson, University of Texas at Arlington


Many librarians fall into the profession because they love their library, and most of us first find that love on the bookshelf. As such, we become some of the most prolific readers and profound critics of the books we read, whether we're deep into biographies or turning over the latest speculative sci-fi to hit the shelf. Yet despite that, our profession affords us little opportunity to really platform our thoughts on the things we've read. Reviews of books about the job of librarianship itself or truncated recommendations for purchase guidance dominate our profession's space for reviews, and while I deeply value my experience in contributing this kind of writing, I always felt that I wasn't scratching that deep itch I have to really review a book. It is my hope that Humanities Methods in Librarianship can afford us the chance to get on our soapbox about the books that have resonated with us or the books that have let us down, to dig into what's happening in the changing genre landscape, or to flex our knowledge and insights as we break down what's happening behind the words on the page. Our relationship with books is not just professional; it is deeply personal and integral to our identity, and we should have the opportunity to write that way.


Kate Villa, National Louis University


The establishment of the new journal, Humanities Methods in Librarianship, critically addresses a gap in the currently existing venues for disseminating ideas in the field of librarianship. Considering how many humanists are drawn to libraries and librarianship, how many library professionals have backgrounds in the humanities, and how, generally speaking, libraries foster our ability to learn and create and provide opportunity for self-discovery and connection, all deeply human endeavors, this project is extremely valuable because it creates that space for researchers in the field of librarianship to share ideas rooted in the humanities.

Unlike a special issue of a general library journal collecting work on a topic related to the humanities, HML is fully dedicated to the domain of humanities scholarship. In a data-driven society that elevates the values of practicality, efficiency, and measurable outcomes, perspectives from the humanities offer insight into the deeper values that underlie the profession. The perspectives can be critical and draw attention to problematic assumptions that drive the progression of librarianship. For many librarians, research output is expected and rewarded for retainment and advancement. It can be alienating when the process of writing and publishing we are expected to do is formulaic and relies on a limited repertoire of methodologies characteristic of the social sciences. I think this journal offers a very important opportunity and venue for humanist scholars who are also librarians to contribute to a growing body of research in librarianship without becoming alienated from the methods and ideas of the humanities where their expertise and academic passion is derived from.

I am excited to participate in this project as a co-editor of the philosophy section because as a librarian with a background in the humanities, I feel alienated from the research skills and interests that I cultivated while completing a PhD in philosophy. Working as an academic librarian, there is often a tacit understanding that professional research not explicitly related to librarianship should be deprioritized. I believe that Humanities Methods in Librarianship is uniquely valuable in that it will provide space for an expanded understanding of what research in librarianship is and can be.


Patrick Williams, Syracuse University


For my Issue 0 idea contribution, I think I’m going to repeat something I mentioned in my application—I believe this journal represents a new kind of space for interesting and emergent work that doesn’t quite have a place elsewhere, and I’m eager to be involved in making that happen. Additionally, I can tell from working with LIS graduate students that they are looking to find the kinds of work HML seeks to publish that engages them and inspires them. I think they find those kinds of things here and there, but to have a publication that is open and welcoming of not-strictly-LIS subject matter and approaches is very exciting to someone entering the field who may have deep interests that lie at the boundaries of LIS and the subjects the journal is attuned to.

item.title: Ode to The Abode of All Known (Issue 1)
item.description:
Ode to the Abode of All Known

by Sean Francis

Publication details

Humanities Methods in Librarianship, Issue 1

Publication date: September 18, 2026

Author details

Chicago, IL, USA.

Id est (i.e.)

The Library.


From any hellscape

a great escape


This place of grace—


Where language

in array


Awaits.


*


Not to scant

pure picture books


(Novel graphics)—


Nor the flat, thick atlas

with its pale-hued maps,


Math texts’ graphs and fractions.


Their name is legion,

The Library’s benefactions.


*


Including

providing


—Access to The Web

—Welcoming Chairs

—Climate Change

—A Private Toilet

—Sinks for Washing Up


To those with no

fixed address:


Who thus can come

as to their home

away from

no home.


*


It’s not quite or always noiseless

there, but closer to than any else—


It’s where silence, enjoined,

is most enjoyed.


*


Let’s us Latin it

for a minute,

our special site:


Locus Amoenus

means “Happy Confine”—


Which thought of

as a paradox


Might remind us

it’s in essence wall-less—


That Library

is a kind of rhyme

for Liberty.


*


Not the least of its felicities

its infrastructure’s lexicon:


—Archive

—Carrel

—Microfiche

—The Stacks

—Dusty Tomes

—Carpeted Hush

—Inkpad with Stamp

—Card Catalogue (alas, rarely seen these days…)


…but from which,

when it existed,

my mother, a librarian,

would bring home cards

for items, I now surmise,

deaccessioned.


These were ubiquitous

in our house,

serving as the chits

for sundry scripts:


—Reminders

—Recipes

—Shopping Lists

—Phone Numbers


All the jottings

of JOF

(Janet Oaks Francis)

as she was known at work—


At home

as Mom.


*


Where would I be?

The Library.


(Where would I be

without The Library?)


Reliably,

The Library.


Bury me

in The Library.


You say you’re

a Library Scientist!?


Get to work at,

command a salary…


from The Library!

Whiz gee—that’s ecstasy!!


*


May this ode

put paid

to what

I’ve owed—


Be my homage, long

OVERDUE.

item.title: Embracing Place and Naming Placelessness in Librarianship (Issue 1)
item.description:
Embracing Place and Naming Placelessness in Librarianship

by Nick Szydlowski

Publication details

Humanities Methods in Librarianship, Issue 1

Publication date: September 16, 2026

Author details

Affiliation: San José State University, San Jose, CA, USA

ORCiD

Keywords:

place; placelessness; re-localizing libraries; colonialism

Abstract:

In response to recent calls to re-localize libraries, this essay takes up the questions of place and placelessness in librarianship and library practice by drawing on approaches to those subjects from a number of fields, including urban studies, philosophy, Native American studies, and postcolonial studies. While re-localization is often considered within discourses of sustainability, the approaches of these humanistic disciplines offer opportunities to broaden the scope of our interest in place and consider how modes of knowledge creation and information seeking can be deeply rooted in place. In particular, by connecting the ethos of placelessness to the history of colonial expansion, work in these fields can help librarians identify ways to nurture a sense of place that is responsive to the experiences of individuals and groups within their user communities. Understanding information and knowledge production as the product of specific places and contexts is a fundamental humanistic insight, but the locality of information is increasingly obscured in information -seeking tools such as search interfaces and chatbots. Developing a richer vocabulary for understanding place and placelessness and reflecting on one’s own relationship to place are possible entry points for librarians in developing a greater focus on place in their practice.

Introduction

Over the past decade, a number of librarians have published calls for libraries to re-localize.1 Often rooted theoretically in movements for sustainable libraries, and for sustainability more generally, these arguments engage the question of how librarians and libraries can cultivate a sense of place in order to counter broader currents that reduce place to mere location, and which treat places as essentially interchangeable, as though one place is as good as another. Viewed through the lens of environmental crisis, care for place, in the form of re-localizing, can be seen as a counter to powerful actors who appear content to flatten the rich diversity of our planet into a global marketplace.


Amy Brunvand makes a particularly compelling case for the idea of re-localizing the library. She contrasts placeless professional approaches that cast libraries as “portals to a globalized and commercialized online knowledge system” with practices focused on place and locality, including “movements within librarianship that place importance on community resilience, cultural diversity and sustainability.”2 Reflecting her commitment to sustainable librarianship, Brunvand situates the question of place, placelessness, and re-localization within the theoretical and historical framework of the Anthropocene. However, discourses of place and placelessness in other academic fields, particularly those in the humanities and those that apply humanities methods in an interdisciplinary context, offer other temporal and theoretical framings for the question of place and placelessness that have the potential to enrich discussions of these topics within librarianship. Scholarship in fields including urban studies, philosophy, Native American studies, and postcolonial studies can help us to situate the question of place in a broader historical context, before the Anthropocene. Scholars in these fields locate the emergence of placelessness in the West much earlier, in currents such as modernism, the Enlightenment, and even the spread of Christianity.


Engaging with concepts of place and placelessness developed in these fields may lead to the conclusion that localizing or re-localizing the library may require or perhaps facilitate a deeper engagement with the philosophical assumptions that shape the field, such as the commitment of libraries to neutrality and the rooting of library values and practices in the European Enlightenment.3 This essay attempts to connect the emerging discourse of re-localizing, with its focus on sustainability, with conversations about place and placelessness in other academic disciplines in order to further explore what it might mean for libraries to re-localize.


More specifically, considering what it would mean for libraries to adopt an ethos of care for place, rather than one of placelessness, requires us to draw on the genealogy of thinking about place in humanities disciplines. The relationship between information, knowledge, and ideas on the one hand, and place on the other, is a fundamentally humanistic question. It engages with core concerns and fundamental insights of the humanities as a whole, and of individual humanities disciplines, including the insight that ideas and concepts originate in specific places and communities, and the insight that subjective modes of communication and experience such as narrative have an important role to play in understanding the way human knowledge is created, experienced, and shared. In order for library and information studies (LIS) to gain a better understanding of the role of place in libraries and in information more broadly, we must adopt humanities methods and turn to scholarship in the humanities that addresses these questions. Moreover, the unique role of LIS as a meta-discipline that concerns itself with information created within other domains of knowledge, including other academic disciplines, opens a door for librarians and LIS researchers to develop methods that bridge disciplines within the humanities to address core questions about the very human endeavor of information seeking and knowledge production.


The conception of LIS as a meta-discipline is developed most completely in the work of Marcia J. Bates, who identifies meta-disciplines as those that address “knowledge in all the conventional fields on the academic spectrum, but [do] so from a particular orientation or position that is needed to accomplish the work and the theorising of its area.”4 Citing Bates, Rong Tang et al. write that “the field of information is a meta-field that cuts across conventional academic disciplines, and its boundary can be configured through practices of cross- and inter-disciplinary engagement with other disciplines.”5 Tang’s description of the field as one whose boundaries are established and possibly changed through interdisciplinary engagement underscores the generative possibilities of engaging with humanities research in an LIS context.


In addressing the specific question of the relationship between information and place, humanities disciplines provide theoretical grounding that is both valuable and highly varied. Trying to understand the relationship between information and place relying solely on frameworks derived from the social sciences and without turning to the humanities would be like entering a fight with one hand, or perhaps both hands, tied behind our backs. It is past time for LIS to take its role as a structurally interdisciplinary meta-discipline more seriously, and to engage with scholarship and insights from the humanities that address core issues in the field.


Remembering Place

It has often been observed that place is an elusive concept, especially in Western world views and philosophies.6 Place cannot be reduced to its precise coordinates like location, or even defined borders, like a country or city. A sense of place may be subjective, and felt or intuited as much as it is known. As an example, researchers studying the boundaries of urban neighborhoods find discrepancies between how different participants draw the lines between different parts of their cities.7


Despite its purported slipperiness, the concept of place has been a subject of academic research in a variety of fields, including philosophy, architecture and urban planning, and postcolonial theory. Within LIS, discussions of place are rare, and the relationship between place and information remains undertheorized. One challenge in advancing ideas about place in LIS is that LIS literature is more likely to adopt an ethos of placelessness, seeking to establish librarianship as a profession whose best practices are absolute and standardized, and not contingent on the subjectivity and specificity of place. While many LIS articles report on local projects and practices, our standard of scholarity dictates that these projects be extrapolated to other contexts as lessons or new recommendations. We reward depicting practice as portable and universal, and rarely focus the attention of the field on projects that are deeply rooted in their local context. In the broader profession, placelessness is an unspoken part of our professional standard.


It is worth pausing to distinguish between different meanings of the term “place.” LIS has produced an active scholarly conversation on the topic of “library as place.”8 However, this literature is, with few exceptions, focused on the physical buildings in which library services are delivered, and the construction of “library as place” is deployed in implicit and often explicit contrast with its antithesis, “library as digital platform.” For example, in introducing the volume Library as Place: Rethinking Roles, Rethinking Space, Kathlin Smith frames the question of library as place as fundamentally related to “the role of the library in the digital age,” asking “what is the role of a library when it no longer needs to be a warehouse of books and when users can obtain information without setting foot in its doors?”9 In discussing online information, placelessness is evoked without being explicitly named, using phrases like “without setting foot,” but the possibility that the physical library may itself reflect an ethos of placelessness is not entertained. Due to its focus on the ways the physical library contrasts with and is disrupted by the digital information environment, the literature of “library as place” cannot provide a complete consideration of the ways libraries and information relate, or might relate to places beyond themselves, such as cities, towns, regions, or neighborhoods. While the impact of technology on the physical spaces of libraries is an important topic, the relationship of libraries to place and placelessness presents a different, largely unexamined set of questions.


These questions are critical because, despite the profession’s commitment to an ethos of placelessness, librarianship remains a stubbornly local and place-bound activity. While there are many exceptions, the vast majority of libraries and librarians do their work in a specific place, for the people who inhabit that place. The attention and care that library workers bring to the local is something we do at times celebrate, especially within individual libraries, but both the academic theory and the financial structures of the field reward work and workers that can easily be transplanted from one library to another.


Similarly, the creation of information—writing, researching, analyzing, synthesizing—has a persistent relationship to place that may be obscured through the interfaces that we construct. The way we organize information, whether online or in the stacks, can flatten this spatial aspect of information in favor of more rationalized and easily searched points of access. While contemporary large language models provide a particularly dramatic example of the ways information and ideas can be radically decontextualized, generative AI is only the latest in a series of technologies that tend to obscure the stubbornly place-bound nature of information, in the pursuit of an ideal or illusion of placelessness.


Placelessness

In order to understand what it might mean to devote more care and attention to place, it is helpful to first explore the concept of placelessness. In particular, looking at how placelessness emerges and evolves as it appears in a few different contexts is one way to enrich our understanding of the role of place in information. Placelessness is not just a carelessness or lack of attention to place; instead, each form of placelessness elevates other values and goals over the concerns of place.


Placelessness in Geography and Urban Planning

In the context of geography and urban planning, Edward Relph observed in Place and Placelessness (1976) that “placelessness is an attitude… which is becoming increasingly dominant,” and as a result, “it is less and less possible to have a deeply felt sense of a place or to create places authentically.”10 Relph’s focus is on a “self-conscious and deliberate” inauthenticity that he argues animates public and social planning in the modernist period.11 In this environment, “objects are manipulated for the public interest and decisions are taken in a world of assumed, homogeneous space and time.”12 For Relph and many subsequent thinkers on place, placelessness can be understood as an orientation to the world that embraces inauthenticity in pursuit of technique, a useful category developed in the work of Jacques Ellul.13 Relph defines technique as “an overriding concern with functional efficiency, objective organisation, and manipulative planning.”14 In this context, the practitioner “subsumes their individuality and that of others to a set of procedures which are determined by the technical nature of social engineering and planning.”15 Relph is careful to argue that this inauthenticity is not inherently worse or better than authenticity, but that its goals and results are quite different.


Technique is a powerful concept to import into librarianship, because it so precisely names the prevailing attitude of the profession. Our reliance on rationality, on procedure and policy, and on an impersonal ethic of neutrality all speak to the centrality of technique to library practice. Relph describes landscapes shaped by technique as “ordered, sometimes blatantly and rigidly ordered, with the lines of good sense adhered to without deviation. It is usually a landscape that has no serious concern with locality and eliminates any traces of its predecessors.”16 However, the placeless attitude, with its focus on technique, is not without its own attractive qualities. For Relph, technique and planning aim to serve what is framed as the public interest, which is expressed in abstract, typically economic terms, and strongly associated with modernist ideals of architecture and design, producing a landscape that, for Relph, expresses “the myths of reason, of the ideal past and the ideal future, of progress and permissiveness, of individual freedom and material comfort.”17 The risk of this inauthenticity, though, is that its rational abstractions and shared myths are “divorced from places as we know and experience them in our everyday lives, and quite casually ignor[e] or obliterat[e] them.”18


While this risk may seem more immediate in the realm of architecture and planning than in libraries and information, it is worth asking if the same framing might apply in our context. How might a librarianship overly focused on technique inflect users’ everyday experiences of reading, learning and research? As a simple example, consider the way the experience of browsing the stacks in an academic library is influenced by design decisions that project objectivity, even in areas shaped by subjective decisions and structures. Picture the labels found on the book stacks at an academic library. In my own experience, these labels contain the call number range of the particular set of shelves, and perhaps a range number, as depicted in Figure 1.

The presentation of the call numbers suggests reason and objectivity. The label itself is legible to some librarians and perhaps to a few experienced researchers, but to everyone else it may as well be a barcode or some other machine-readable format. What if the labels included a few words to capture the contents of the range? How would that change the character of the library, or the experience of researchers? One change might be that these text descriptions would bring subjectivity, and perhaps even eccentricity, into the context of the library stacks. While some ranges would be easy to describe, others might challenge the creativity of the employees charged with creating the descriptions for heterogenous materials.


While we might imagine labels that bring some joy or lightness to the experience of browsing, or that use language designed to be easily understood by users of a specific library, undermining the presentation of objectivity may have other implications in this context. Call numbers are not, of course, merely codes that indicate the physical location of an item, but instead reflect systems of subject classification—systems that encode power relationships through the organization of information.19 While critical approaches to cataloging and metadata are increasingly widespread within libraries, in the example at hand, neither the subjectivity of classification nor the power relationships at play are legible in the dry, technocratic code of the call number range.20 It may even offer an opportunity for some libraries to use the space of the stack end to surface these dynamics.


Rather than intervening in conversations about classification or making any kind of generalized recommendation for how libraries might improve the browsing experience, the purpose of this example is to demonstrate what it might mean to apply Relph’s critique of placelessness in the built environment to library spaces and services, and to imagine local changes that might foster a sense of place. Conceptions of placelessness developed in geography and urban studies can provide a way of reading the environments that libraries create, and becoming sensitive to the ways the design of a space, service, or website projects objectivity, neutrality, or placelessness. Analyzing and attending to these instances may be a first step on a path to re-localizing.


Placelessness in Philosophy, Intellectual History, and Native American Studies

While Relph associates placelessness with a modernist orientation that dates to the twentieth century, Edward S. Casey’s The Fate of Place: A Philosophical History locates the evolution of placelessness much earlier.21 In this comprehensive account of philosophical discourses on place in the Western tradition, Casey outlines the development, between approximately 400 BC and 1800 AD, of an orientation focused on the universal and on a conception of space as both universal and infinite. For Casey, this orientation largely supplanted earlier perspectives focused on place, and on the importance of local knowledge and customs. Importantly, this new placelessness is not contained in a single philosophical or institutional context, but forms a bridge between Christian theology and the scientific worldview of the Enlightenment:

The colonizing tendency of Christianity is echoed in the attempts of Galilean, Cartesian, and Newtonian physics to appropriate whole realms formerly consigned to alchemy and “natural philosophy,” not to mention local custom and history. In both instances, the power of place, uncontested in the ancient world (and still potently present in medieval times), was put in abeyance—indeed, often literally abolished, and with as much relentless force as that with which native peoples were subjected to Christian indoctrination.22

Casey draws an explicit link between Christian theology and Enlightenment physics, and demonstrates that link in particular through the writings of the philosopher Henry More, an important influence on Isaac Newton, who posited both space and God as “infinitely extended albeit incorporeal substances.”23 Casey argues that, at least in its relationship to place, physics builds on, rather than contradicts, Christian theology. Here the focus on place calls into question portrayals of the European Enlightenment as a rejection of Christian dogma, perhaps most famously embodied in Brecht’s The Life of Galileo. For Casey, the development of placelessness is a shared project of the Enlightenment and European Christianity.


The connection Casey draws between placelessness and colonialism is equally striking, and his work benefits from being read in conversation with other recent scholarship that attempts to reshape narratives of intellectual history in general and the Enlightenment in particular. David Graeber and David Wengrow’s The Dawn of Everything: A New History of Humanity also hinges on our imagination of the Enlightenment and in particular its relationship to colonialism.24 A key element in their argument is what they call the Indigenous critique of European culture, a clearly articulated intellectual current, expressed by thinkers and intellectuals indigenous to the Americas in response to contact with Europeans. One expression of this critique comes through the thought of the Wendat leader Kandiaronk, whose ideas were captured in a widely read series of debates published by French aristocrat Louis Armand, Baron de Lahontan.25 Graeber and Wengrow argue that the Indigenous critique plays an essential and overlooked role in introducing concern with equality and freedom into the European discourse on politics and the state.26 In particular, they trace the influence of this critique on the work of Rousseau and on the French and American revolutions, and argue that “Europeans learned from Native Americans about the connection between reasoned debate, personal freedoms and the refusal of arbitrary power.”27


In making these arguments, Graeber and Wengrow build on the work of Donald A. Grinde Jr. and Bruce E. Johansen, who documented the direct influence of Iroquois forms of government on the drafting of the United States Constitution. Grinde and Johansson focus primarily on the intellectual formation of the United States, but they argue more broadly that “during the Enlightenment, Europe took new knowledge about the ordering of human affairs from all over the world,” but especially from North America.28 They contend that “in essence, American democracy is a synthesis of Native American and European political theories.”29 In presenting their evidence, they underscore that this synthesis was widely understood and remarked upon at the time, and only came to be obscured in later, more Euro-centric narratives.


This story of Native American influence on Western thought is a powerful illustration of what can be gained by approaching information and knowledge with a sensitivity to place. Graeber and Wengrow catalog several forms in which the Indigenous critique was published and widely read in Europe, including accounts of colonial missionaries and fictionalized accounts of the responses that newcomers from America might have when first encountering European society. However, the fact that these works were in most cases credited to European authors and published through European modes of information sharing continues to complicate the claim that the underlying ideas contained in the Indigenous critique originated in the Americas. In questioning Graeber and Wengrow’s reliance on these sources, Robbie Richardson asks the key question about the statements attributed to Kandiaronk: “Do these texts truly grant access to Indigenous thought?”30 From a librarian’s point of view, the difficulty—and perhaps the impossibility—of answering this question, of trying to understand which resources or texts might reliably represent historical Indigenous perspectives and which are merely the projections of Europeans, demonstrates an example of an information environment that has failed to accurately or reliably record the sources of ideas.


However, the concept of the Indigenous critique need not rest solely on the ideas that Graeber and Wengrow attribute to Kandiaronk. Richardson himself is “sympathetic to the claim that Indigenous people produced one of the key conceptual shifts in the European Enlightenment,” and the work of Grinde and Johansen, focusing on the intellectual foundations of the United States government rather than the Enlightenment more generally, makes similar claims on the basis of different historical sources.31 Still, claims like the Indigenous critique, which address not just the contents of specific texts but the origins of ideas and intellectual currents, must rely on an information environment that preserves those origins. When considering our current information environment, the risk seems even more severe that ideas that originated in specific places and communities may quickly be carried away from their places of origin, with the attendant loss of both attribution and surrounding intellectual context.


Returning to Casey, is there a way to reconcile these two views of the Enlightenment, in particular with regard to their treatment of place and placelessness? For Casey, the elevation of space and universality over place and specificity is a key marker of this period in the intellectual history of Europe. He draws connections between colonial expansion and the imaginary of the infinite and the unbounded. This orientation may help make sense of the fate of the Indigenous critique, and the ease with which the ideas it contained slipped free of their origin in a particular place—the northeast corner of the Americas—and came to be associated with more abstract and universalist expressions. In this telling, the Indigenous critique emerges as a set of organic observations, rooted not just in a single culture, but in a specific encounter or juxtaposition. Yet that context is obscured, as the critique is incorporated into political theories that imagine the human condition to be universal, rather than specific and place-bound. It is placelessness that removes the Native American origins of this critique and allows us to imagine it as a European philosophy.


Within library science, the Enlightenment and its meaning for libraries has become a site of some contestation. Wayne Bivens-Tatum writes that “the philosophical and political principles of the European Enlightenment provide the philosophical foundation of American academic and public libraries.”32 The Enlightenment lineage has been employed both as a critique and a defense of the intellectual foundations of library praxis. nina de jesus argues that the library’s inheritance from the Enlightenment is not primarily a set of ideas about individual liberty but an ideology that produced and enabled systemic oppression across the globe in the form of white supremacy and settler colonialism.33 In contrast, John Wenzler relies on this lineage to argue for the continued value of neutrality as a value and ethical imperative for librarians.34 Wenzler points out that both he and de jesus root their arguments in the idea that the genealogy of libraries runs back to the Enlightenment. But what happens to these arguments if we do take seriously the claim that Enlightenment ideas are not as purely European as we might have imagined them to be, but instead have their origins, at least in part, in Native American intellectual traditions? If we separate out the placeless, universalist thread of thought traced by Casey from the Indigenous critique outlined by Graeber and Wengrow, we might argue that de jesus and Wenzler are not, in fact, addressing the same set of intellectual currents when they appeal to the Enlightenment. The Enlightenment that de jesus rejects corresponds more closely to the placeless thread that Casey connects to colonial expansion; the Enlightenment that Wenzler embraces may represent a different intellectual tradition, one that only emerged as a result of the encounter between Native Americans and Europeans. While arguments based in a genealogy of libraries are attractive, the ground beneath these arguments may be less stable and more contested than we imagine. On the other hand, any hypothetical attempt to apply Graeber and Wengrow’s work to defend or reimagine the Enlightenment origins of libraries must contend with the failure of libraries to preserve a definitive record of the historical Indigenous critique, and to ask what critical perspectives we may be failing to preserve in the present.


While Casey describes a European philosophical tradition moving away from a focus on place and toward a form of placelessness, scholars working in the field of Native American Studies may be more likely to posit placelessness as a quality of Western thought as a whole, and to emphasize the importance of place in indigenous cultures. Mishuana Goeman emphasizes the role of narrative in creating place, writing that “there are many examples of the ways in which Indigenous people make place through stories. Relationships between land and people are complex and nuanced and shaped from our personal interactions with our environment as well as through collected communal memories.”35 Goeman contrasts this understanding of place with a set of other ways of understanding it: as personal property; as the site of political contestation and state sovereignty; and even as a mode of containment, as the essay contemplates the location of prisons on historical sites of confrontation.


Jay T. Johnson’s account of the concept of the storied landscape makes the relationship between place and knowledge production even more explicit. Johnson proposes two ways of understanding place: “first, place as a way of understanding, knowing, and learning about the world; and second as the embodied location of everyday struggle for meaning.”36 Johnson argues that the storied landscape itself is a form of library, a repository for forms of knowledge recorded and transmitted through place-based narratives.


The notion of place as shaped and defined through narrative practice or as a library of knowledge shared through narratives about specific places is an emphatic example of what it can mean for an intellectual tradition to foreground place. It may be helpful to contrast this conception of place as inseparable from the process of creating and transmitting knowledge with a conception that reduces place to merely or simply a quantifiable location in space. This contrast may help to demonstrate why surfacing the question of place and placelessness may prove helpful in understanding and reconciling the different intellectual traditions that are present in libraries and in our information environment more broadly.


The question of how we understand the intellectual origins of major developments like the Enlightenment or the United States Constitution demonstrates at a macro level the stakes of place within information science and librarianship. In an imagined, idealized library, a user should not only be able to discover facts—the text of the Constitution—but also to access ideas and their origins or attributions. Of course, the origins of ideas will always be contested, but users should also be able to discover those sites of contestation and inform themselves on the state of intellectual contestation.


This is true not only of famous historical moments, but also of the myriad more granular topics of inquiry and contestation that make up the scope of human research and expression. Just as we can ask, “Where did the ideas behind the Enlightenment originate?” we can also ask about the context—not just the location, but the place—where any idea or perspective originates. If we accept the argument, made by Graeber and Weingrow, and before them by Grinde and Johansen, that the catalyst for the Enlightenment was the encounter between Europeans and Native Americans, we arrive at a very different understanding of the Enlightenment itself. It was not necessarily a European phenomenon, but instead represented the importation of Native American ideas about freedom, hierarchy, and political organization into a European context in which they were novel and even revolutionary. From this perspective, we can start to see how place might shape information and ideas in more fundamental ways than we typically imagine. Could it be that it was only in a specific set of places and times—pockets of North America in the colonial era—that a mix of individuals and cultures created the conditions for the cultural synthesis that we now call the Enlightenment?


Importantly, the most powerful infrastructure for sharing these new perspectives primarily existed in European capitals. As a result, the Native American influence that these scholars insist on, and that they argue was clearly articulated and acknowledged at the time, has faded from the scholarly record. But there are other kinds of records and histories. Grinde and Johansen write that

American Indian people in their scholarship and tribal traditions … clearly perceive the history of North America as interactive and a product of synthesis. Print-oriented scholars who ignore this understanding of North American history tend to amplify the divisiveness, racism, violence, and segregation that developed out of the eventual domination of European culture.37

The phrase “print-oriented scholars,” and its analog, “print-oriented librarians,” is key here. In this context, “print-oriented” does not mean attached to print books as opposed to digital ones, but attached to print, to text, to books and articles, as opposed to other ways of knowing and sharing information. Perhaps in turning attention to place, librarians will find that that the histories and cultures of many—perhaps most—places are poorly documented in the print record. We may even find that other forms—traditional forms like oral storytelling and community archiving and collecting, as well as emerging forms like mapping and digital storytelling38—are more suited to creating and preserving information resources related to particular places and contexts. Within the profession, some of these practices may be framed as applications of emerging technologies, but perhaps we would be better served by considering the ways these practices apply much older approaches, such as the creation and preservation of knowledge through the relationship between stories and places.


Place in Postcolonial Studies

As we have already seen, foregrounding place can lead quickly to a concern for the history of specific places and ideas that in turn can lead to a consideration of major structures, like colonialism, that have shaped those histories. Within the field of postcolonial studies, however, some scholars note a strong suspicion of considerations of place, which may be attributed to “the strategic uses to which the notion of place has been put over the course of colonial history.”39 In the postcolonial context, the human relationship to place is often shattered, sometimes repeatedly, as people are literally displaced, or as places are renamed and transformed through occupation. As Tosin Gbogi writes:

Places can oppress places, but since these exist in a natural world that is borderless, it is more appropriate to say that humans manipulate places and endow them with meanings that generate harmonious as well as antagonistic relations. The colonial production of place worked mostly in this way.40

Understanding place as a primary means of ongoing colonial control and influence, as Gbogi does, complicates the project of developing and articulating one’s own relationship to place, and the expression and analysis of this ambivalence toward place is a critical and distinctive feature of postcolonial literature and of the scholarship that studies it.


In considering how, or if, postcolonial studies may be relevant to relationships to place in countries shaped by settler colonialism, it is important to balance criticisms levied against the field as insufficiently attuned to the structures of settler colonialism with the applicability of its insights to the experiences and orientations to place of individual library users.41 Taking the United States as an example, while the government and power structures of the country are more accurately described as setter colonial than postcolonial, the personal relationships of individuals—library users—to colonialism may take many forms. For example, a library user in the United States may locate themself as both a settler on Native American land and as a person displaced from their own ancestral home due to colonialism.42 Each of these perspectives may shape that user’s relationship to place. When considering possible orientations to place, the insights of postcolonial studies have applications for understanding individual orientations and experiences, even in settings where structures of colonial power persist.


In tracing scholarly approaches to place in the field of postcolonial studies, Eric Prieto distinguishes between a more space-oriented or universalist group, whom he refers to as neo-Marxists, and a place-oriented group, who he dubs culturalists. The neo-Marxists “describe a global space segmented into geopolitical territories but shaped increasingly by an abstract network of economic forces that is able to cross national borders with ease.43 In contrast, the culturalists argue that “any totalizing theory claiming to have universal jurisdiction is bound to have unforeseen implications when transported from one cultural context to another.44 Prieto credits the culturalist position with seeking a middle ground

between the extremes of ethnocentrism and universalism, in which the concept of place has a critical role to play. By emphasizing the ways in which geographical identities cut transversally through ethnic and social (class) affiliations, their work makes it possible to convey a sense of place as a base from which cultural differences can be preserved in the face of globalization and standardization without succumbing to the exclusionary and discriminatory temptations evoked by both the neo-Marxists and the universalizing humanists.45

The postcolonial lens, then, complicates our conceptions of both place and placelessness by emphasizing the ways in which our relationships to these contexts are shaped by history and power. Placelessness may exist not only as a choice or orientation, as in the Western philosophical discourse discussed earlier, but as a condition imposed upon an individual or a people. However, by outlining the many relationships to place expressed through the postcolonial tradition, Prieto demonstrates that placelessness—an ambivalence toward or rejection of the experience of place as place—is not synonymous, or even necessarily correlated with statelessness or exile. George B. Handley captures this dynamic in an essay on the work of the poet Derek Walcott:

The problem is that the very locale of the postcolonial subject has in fact been determined by imperial powers. Therefore, the postcolonial subject is not only placed in a discontinuous relation to the imperatives of European colonialism and history, but is also placed in a problematic relation to land since land represents both the site of one’s emotional and cultural development and perhaps of one’s history of displacement and alienation.46

For librarians in the Americas, engagement with place cannot be simple. Handley reminds us that what may appear to be

a moral crisis of placelessness can also be understood as a political crisis as well if we consider the displacement and murder of Native Americans, the violent transplantation of Africans, and the chaotic scattering of many Europeans, Asians, and others in New World history, factors that have all been more difficult to ignore in areas like the Caribbean.47

By recentering discourse on places—like the Caribbean—where the impacts of colonialism are most immediately visible and least easily disguised, the postcolonial discourse on place forces us to notice the way our own locales, and our own histories, have been shaped by the same violent and chaotic forces.


In applying the insights of postcolonial scholarship to professional practice in our library, I often refer to the work of Roopika Risam, which encompasses postcolonial studies and digital humanities approaches. Risam writes that

digital humanities, as a field, can only be inclusive and its diversity can only thrive in an environment in which local specificity—the unique concerns that influence and define digital humanities at regional and national levels—is positioned at its center and its global dimensions are outlined through an assemblage of the local.48

The orientation Risam suggests for digital humanities can also be applied to librarianship, with the implication that the profession can embrace the diversity of local practice and define itself not through the placeless lens of technique, standards, or best practices, but as an assemblage of locally specific approaches and concerns.


More broadly, however, the discourse on place that emerges from postcolonial studies complicates the relationship between place and placelessness by foregrounding experiences of violence, displacement, and exile that may introduce a specific mode of ambivalence around the concept of place. One expression of this perspective comes through explorations of postcolonial cosmopolitanism.49 In a reading of the work of Frantz Fanon, Julian Go writes that “Fanon’s postcolonial cosmopolitan embraces and advocates a worldwide citizenship, a global humanity, in dialogue with the fact that European imperialism and its associated exploitations and dominations have so long repressed such humanity. It [is] in the spaces that colonialism left behind that [the] postcolonial cosmopolitan emerges.”50 Postcolonial cosmopolitanism emerges quite literally from a different place, or set of places, than more widely discussed forms of cosmopolitanism that originate in Europe and parallel the intellectual currents of placelessness.


Synthesizing Place and Placelessness across Disciplines

Rather than helping us arrive at a single understanding of place and placelessness, examining the way these concepts play out in different academic disciplines and discourses can serve to illustrate the many resonances and potential meanings of place. As a core component of human experience, place cannot be made simple.
