Seen in this way, a pattern begins to emerge that associates placelessness with the philosophical and ideological currents that undergirded European colonialism, along with later intellectual currents such as modernism and technological solutionism. However, work in postcolonial studies provides an important counter-pattern, especially through the concept of postcolonial cosmopolitanism. Seen through this lens, it may not be possible to recover a precolonial relationship to place. It may not be possible to separate place from its role as a physical site of colonial extraction.


Writing in a postcolonial context, many literary authors have turned to the figure of a precolonial Eden or paradise. Sharae Deckard finds that “throughout this literature, paradise begins as a geographical topos motivating European exploration and colonization, evolves into a myth justifying imperial discourse and praxis, and finally becomes an ironic motif responding to neo-colonialism and global capitalism.”51 In one way of understanding this construction, postcolonial subjects inhabit a fallen world, in which there is no hope of regaining a prelapsarian relationship to place. In this context, one’s relationship to place becomes more complex, perhaps layered in irony or marked by painful history.


Building on the idea that place can shape ideas and information, perhaps one way of reconciling these different positions is to consider the types of places, and by extension the perspectives, that are foregrounded by each of these disciplines. The different associations with place and placelessness that we see in Indigenous studies and postcolonial studies reflect different relationships to place produced by different localized historical experiences. If libraries are to effectively re-localize, we must consider that different library users will seek out or be open to different ways of relating to and engaging with place.


Here Bates’ conception of LIS as a meta-discipline is of particular importance.52 Librarians and LIS researchers do not necessarily need to consistently choose one particular disciplinary framing or set of associations when developing an understanding of how place shapes information. We do not necessarily need to choose, either as a field or as individuals, the framing of Indigenous studies over that of postcolonial studies or vice versa. We have the opportunity instead to frame each of these approaches as valid within their respective communities of practice, as different ways of developing and shaping knowledge on the concept of place. LIS scholarship may then serve, just as the library itself does, as a space where different disciplinary perspectives interface and exist beside one another. Michael Dudley writes that “as a meta-discipline, LIS can afford the scholar a catholic perspective on research problems external to librarianship itself, one potentially liberated from internecine debates and disciplinary conventions that might constrain other scholars.”53 The meta-disciplinary perspective of LIS presents opportunities to productively synthesize and compare the perspectives of different fields on issues relevant to libraries and information. This meta-disciplinary perspective is as applicable to practice as it is to research, carrying the potential to support a highly localized approach to library practice. In engaging with place, some libraries may find a particular disciplinary approach to be more relevant in their context, and to the communities that they serve. A complete understanding of the ways people relate to place and the ways place may in turn inflect their experience of information cannot be captured by a single discipline or tradition, but both research and practice in LIS represent sites where the understandings of different disciplines can coexist in synthesis and contrast.


Libraries as Sites of Engagement with Place

While I would argue that the practice of librarianship is almost unavoidably engaged with place, discussions of place in librarianship tend to focus more narrowly on collecting and programming related to local history. Many library users wishing to build and engage with a sense of place may take an interest in local history, and some local history programs both within and outside of libraries explicitly address their impact on participants’ sense of place.54 However, the concept of local history is one that may resonate in different ways for different library users. For community archives in particular, subjective impressions of places and communities may shift over time as “community archives users form and utilize their imaginaries both to continually define their communities, by negotiating and imagining elastic boundaries, and to anticipate future shifts in the boundaries of their communities.”55 The question of community boundaries—of whose stories are included and whose excluded—is relevant not only for community archives organized within marginalized communities, but for all local history collections. The intertwined concerns—that North American archival collections fail to reflect the histories of marginalized communities and that they fail to reflect ordinary people in general—date back at least fifty years.56


Local history, then, is a contested space in which multiple groups and points of view co-exist. From the perspective of the United States, this may reflect the reality of the Americas, shaped by colonialism, where both individual and group relationships to place can be complex and sometimes contradictory. In this context local history programs may benefit from considering the complex currents that shape the places they seek to document, or even imagining themselves as spaces in which conflicts and differences of perspective are permitted to surface. Moreover, for many individuals, their own relationship to place may be eccentric or personal, and therefore not reflected even at the margins of the space we call history.


Engagement with place is not synonymous with parochialism or nativism, and this is particularly true when multiple ways of thinking about place are cultivated. One reason to ground our work in this area in a wide range of scholarship, and in fields like Native American and postcolonial scholarship in particular, is to broaden our sense of the ways librarians and library users may relate to place. Our relationships to a particular place may be emphatic or ambivalent, new or deeply rooted, knowledgeable or naive, affectionate or critical. All of these possible orientations, though, differ categorically from the orientation of placelessness, which proposes that one place is as good as another, and that all of these relationships are merely sentimental distractions from a rational, technical approach to the work of libraries.


One way to think about localizing or re-localizing the library may be to imagine or reimagine libraries as sites that facilitate or encourage engagement with place. In order to support and cultivate the rich diversity of possible relationships to place, libraries and librarians would need to go about re-localizing in a way that supports authentic, varied and personal relationships to place. Here Relph is helpful in identifying inauthentic approaches to place, and in particular highlighting the style and attitude of kitsch, in which “the trivial is made significant and the significant is made trivial.”57 While it is easy to identify kitsch in tourist gift shops and chamber of commerce advertising, libraries adopting a program of re-localization must be careful to avoid repeating familiar narratives that elevate superficial symbols of place above the subjective individual experience of place.


Perhaps, then, an important step in any shift toward a more place-oriented practice is individual reflection on one’s own relationship to place. This type of reflection may be particularly valuable for library workers who don’t typically consider their own relationship to place. In that spirit I would propose to situate this argument with a brief personal reflection. I have throughout my life experienced a deep connection with the place in which I was raised: the city of Boston, Massachusetts. As a young musician and aspiring writer, the city featured prominently in my creative work in songwriting and fiction, and in my own sense of my place in the world. Libraries played a significant part in developing my personal imaginary of Boston, with the exhibits at the Norman B. Leventhal Map & Education Center at the Boston Public Library making a permanent impression on my sense of the city. Less romantically, my time as a preservation assistant in the MIT Libraries often found me hunched over damaged government documents from the urban renewal period, and details from those documents shaped my understanding of the city’s history and built environment.


Later, in my early forties, circumstances caused me to relocate, somewhat suddenly, to the Bay Area in California. Here I noticed something unexpected. The manner in which I relate to Boston seemed surprisingly transferable. That is to say, I found myself seeking out a relationship with my new place, and I gravitated toward the ways of relating to the place that I had absorbed in Boston. Here, too, I am drawn to learn more about the complex and violent history of the place where I find myself, and to try to use that sense of place to understand the things I see.


I share this reflection to underscore that relationship to place is not merely relationship to any specific place—to home, or the place one feels most connected to. There are other places as well—places or exile, of immigration, of convenience, of fascination. On an individual level, engagement with place entails the development of a rich internal and perhaps external vocabulary for one’s own relationship with the places one encounters. Even more powerfully, we can build on this vocabulary to better understand the relationships that others have to place, and to particular places.


Placelessness, on the other hand, favors a dulling of this internal sense, seeing it as a source of friction that slows the transmission of people, capital, or (most relevant for libraries) information, through uniform, decontextualized channels. It favors environments that flatten or caricature the distinctive cultures of places, erasing or simplifying their histories.


The way one develops a sense of place may be idiosyncratic, but it is also deeply cultural. As Casey, Johnson, and Goeman argue, the alienation from place that develops into the placelessness of our current era is deeply rooted in certain strains of Western and colonial philosophy and ideology.58 Placelessness itself originates from a specific place. The same is true of other ideas, and of information in general.


Returning to Relph, whose work on place and placelessness formed our starting point, it is notable that he refuses to argue that an engagement with place is superior to placelessness. His work instead focuses on naming and differentiating these two phenomena. We may need to articulate, then, why placelessness is a particularly unproductive orientation for libraries. As a field, we have neglected to notice the extent to which libraries are sites where relationship to place is fostered and cultivated. Place is not only a subject, the topic of some subset of library resources. Relationship to place is a fundamental human capacity and one that—especially in areas like the Americas, which bear the scars of displacement and colonialism—requires cultivation. Fostering this capacity is a fundamental but unstated function of both public and academic libraries. An atmosphere of placelessness threatens our ability to serve this function.


More broadly, foregrounding place and placelessness in the professional and scholarly context of libraries has the potential to bridge theory and practice in a way that speaks directly to the material realities of librarianship. This framework provides an opportunity to build on critiques of neoliberal and authoritarian currents affecting the profession by arguing for the viability and value of practices rooted in the needs and cultures of specific places and user communities. It also creates possibilities for discourses of culture and lived experience that are more specific and more varied, avoiding the pitfalls of essentialism, tokenism, and kitsch.


Libraries already provide sites where users can develop and enrich their ability to relate to places—not only their current place, but any place they may remember or encounter. We do this through collections, of course, but also through active programming. What we rarely do is conceptualize our role in this process. We rarely think of a relationship to place as one of the human capacities we support. Naming this capacity also gives us an opportunity to approach it more thoughtfully, and to draw on the many fields of scholarship that address the ways people relate to places and the ways history and power shape those relationships.


Nor do we name placelessness in our field. Naming placelessness presents an opportunity as well, for with this vocabulary we may point out policies and practices that flatten the distinctiveness of our libraries and the user groups they serve. The discourse of placelessness is particularly urgent in our current technological environment. The increasing application of generative AI in information seeking contexts normalizes the practice of decontextualizing information. As knowledge and information created by human beings in specific locations and contexts is removed from physical space and encoded into the vector space employed by large language models, the connection between information and place is further obscured. While this is merely one of many salient critiques that may be leveled against AI, it illustrates the way our information environment may develop according to an ethos of placelessness. In discussing concepts like the Indigenous critique and postcolonial cosmopolitanism, we have seen concrete examples of how ideas emerge from specific places and contexts, and of how this connection between knowledge and place can change how an idea is received or understood. The practice of disconnecting knowledge not only from its place of origin, but from the physical source or document in which it appears is not a neutral one, but is instead part of the flattening, universalist ethos of placelessness.


Lastly, understanding the complex currents of place and placelessness requires the application of methods and knowledge from disciplines in the humanities that have a long history of engagement with these topics. The position of LIS as a meta-discipline provides a platform on which to engage with complex research in a way that resonates with the diverse perspectives that library users and information seekers bring to the experience of place.

item.title: Pretend It’s Magic: The Story of a Library Management System (Issue 1)
item.description:
Pretend It’s Magic: The Story of a Library Management System

by Tara Kunesh

Publication details

Humanities Methods in Librarianship, Issue 1

Publication date: September 18, 2026

Author details

Affiliation: Georgia Public Library Service, Atlanta, GA, USA.

I’m dancing in a club in Melbourne, Australia. It’s a dimly lit underground establishment not too far from St. Kilda beach where I have been sharing a small apartment with a friend I met sailing. Lights the color of a rich port wine are dotted unevenly upon the walls, and most of the patrons are grouped in corners or leaning over small tables conversing intently. It’s almost midnight on the final night of the 1990s. It’s the type of place that invokes intensity at the best of times and, tonight, the mood is impassioned bordering on overwrought with a side of inebriation. The group of women next to me on the dance floor are sobbing into their Manhattans. When I enquire about their wellbeing, they raise tear-streaked faces that sparkle strangely in the burgundy glow. They glance at their watches. In twenty minutes, they say, life, as we know it, is possibly over. A slightly less weepy woman stares deeply into my eyes. Our jobs, she says, may be no more. Nodding, I back away. I don’t have a job so there’s that. And, well, if the world is going to end, I’m going to take Prince’s advice and party like it’s 1999. Which it is. I turn to the bartender and order another pitcher of vodka and red bull.


Rewind time a little and switch locations. In the United States, the Georgia Public Library Service (GPLS) had been spending the last few years of the nineties thinking much more soberly about the dawn of the next millennium. To be precise, they were thinking about the date January 1st, 2000, technically a year earlier than the new millennium, but let’s not get too bogged down with details. One specific problem they were facing was the fact that many libraries across Georgia were operating with systems that might not be compliant with the potential computer errors that Y2K predicted. The librarians were scrambling for a solution. In 1998, a universal borrowing card for Georgia that would link local library regions into an ambitious state-wide network had been proposed and accepted.1 As such an arrangement would not work unless there was a single integrated library system (ILS) put into place to connect all these disparate libraries, GPLS had also been busy building the Public Information Network for Electronic Services (PINES) to provide such unity and to combine all willing public libraries in Georgia into a resource-sharing consortium.2 PINES rose judiciously from the ashes of anxiety in December 1999 and began life with ninety-eight libraries under its care.


It’s inspirational, and a little humiliating, to think about this work going on while I was drinking cocktails in an Antipodean bar. Seeing as Atlanta, Georgia is fourteen hours behind Melbourne, Australia, there’s even a good chance that the PINES team were hard at work while I danced the (sort-of) millennium away. I’d like to believe that was the case. You see, as I twirled in that infernal glow (averting my gaze from the now almost hysterical group of women), and the DJ counted down to midnight, the Fates were already plotting my circuitous route to Georgia.


I don’t think it will come as much of a spoiler if I say that the world woke up on January 1, 2000, not much worse for wear. There were issues with a few credit card companies, some wonky spreadsheet formulae and the like, but we certainly had not come to the “End of Times.” While Prince was correct to sing that we were all going to die one day, that day was, for many, still somewhere in the hazy future.


The new millennium did signal the end of my sojourn in Australia, however. I had been enjoying their hospitality courtesy of a yearlong visa, and I had almost overstayed my welcome. I took the time offered almost to the minute before dragging myself away from that gorgeous country. This is where Fate rubbed her hands together and got to work. I am not sure to this day why she took an interest and intervened, but it certainly seems that I spent the next year making some atypical decisions. You might think, for example, that I would fly home after being away from my family for approximately three hundred and sixty-seven days (give or take some truly heinous flight times). However, I felt uncommonly ready for a new adventure and decided to head in the opposite direction. Going home for me would have meant returning to England and, instead, I headed to the west coast of America. I fell asleep in a park in downtown San Francisco - waking to find a chattering squirrel perched on my shoulder - before recuperating from the flight in that foggy utopia. Closing my eyes and drawing a dot on the map later in the week determined that my next steps would be to head south to Hollywood.


Most journeys begin with the literal opening of a door. I had been an avid reader of Tolkien when I was around sixteen and remembered that, in both The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, Gandalf the Wizard tries to warn both his heroes–Bilbo and Frodo–of the dangers that lurk beyond the safety of the hearth. While unlikely, there just might be dragons waiting outside. It is then arguable that you would only have yourself to blame for the inevitable fire-blowing, bone-crunching, death-inducing devastation that follows your tentative foray into the wide blue yonder. It’s equally possible, of course, that you might step outside to a scene of delightful tranquility. You might walk forwards in a gentle spill of afternoon sunlight, brushing your hands over an array of waving grasses underneath a baby blue sky. The point is that you don’t know what you will find when you open the door and take that first step. You might board a train at the edge of an ocean that will, eventually, take you somewhere you never planned or expected to be.


We’ll fast forward a little here. My life is really quite incidental to this story. It is enough, perhaps, to explain that, while staying in a hostel in the Hollywood Hills, I met an American man. It’s an immigration tale as old as time; it was far easier to get married in haste and, after twenty-five years, there’s no need to discuss whether I needed to repent at leisure. We tried on lives in England, then Florida, Wyoming, and Utah, before landing in Georgia in the summer of 2012. I still remember the feeling of wonder as I stepped off the plane and felt, for the very first time, the smothering, sweat-inducing blanket of humidity that Atlanta was wrapping cozily around me. I had grown up a little in the last twelve years, and my life was very different. I spent less time in bars and more time scrubbing dirt off my two daughters, throwing child-friendly pasta dishes in the oven, and picking bits of the same pasta dishes out of the carpet.


Meanwhile, back at the PINES ranch, business was booming, although the intervening period had not been without its challenges. At the time of the 1999 launch, PINES had, you may remember, ninety-eight libraries under its electronic wing. Within a year or so, this number had more than doubled. However, while PINES was cheerfully expanding–demonstrating the power of collaboration and sharing–the software behind PINES labored fruitlessly to keep up with such unprecedented growth. There is an infamous day, noted in the literature and remembered by PINES staff, when this software failed completely, resulting in a complete and inconvenient halt to the servers.3 Hearsay adds a layer of bitterness to this era. PINES staff, even now, do not like to mention this software company. If they say its name at all, it is in hushed, furtive whispers. The name has taken on the significance of that equally unmentionable Scottish play. Thankfully, by the time I arrived in Georgia, PINES had left that unhelpful software in the dust and were well into their journey with a new, attractive in-house developed alternative.4 But wait. That statement is a bit of a spoiler and doesn’t really do justice to the drama and boldness of their venture. We need to take a closer look.


Obviously, PINES desired expansion. They wanted more libraries across Georgia to join their consortium. But the fact of the matter was that there simply wasn’t any software on the market that met their needs. It was definitely a moment for PINES to consider whether or not to open that door. Even if there weren’t actual dragons outside, Frodo could have told them a thing or two about other dangers they might find on the road: giant, flesh-eating spiders, zombie horsemen, and whip-wielding demons for starters. PINES opened the door anyway, and in 2004, embarked upon a quest to create their own library management system.5 It seemed a tall order and certainly a leap of faith. I wish I had been around for those conversations. I can only imagine the inordinate level of calculated coaxing it must have taken to convince those in charge that this bold idea was viable. I’ve been adding a lot of analogies about heroic journeys, and you may scoff. But, truly, the creation of the PINES developed, open-source software called Evergreen had the high drama and magical elements befitting an epic quest. Thanks to their powers of persuasion, PINES were allocated two years: They would need to deliver a fully functioning library management system by 2006.6


PINES is—and I am sure was—a closeknit crew. As a cohesive unit, they traipsed around Georgia, inviting library staff to focus groups to discuss the potential software. It was hard, they explained, to get people to think outside the parameters of other systems and what they had seen before. “Pretend it’s magic,”7 the PINES staff urged, encouraging the focus group participants to imagine a library management system that soared above the rest. The PINES team didn’t want to be constrained by previous or known entities; they wanted to develop something extraordinary. “Pretend its magic” is such a lovely concept. What if we used this idea more in life? Do you want a different career? A different spouse? Do you want to move to a different country? Or do you want to own miniature goats? What would you change if you could reach into the fabric of the universe and manipulate its ineffable mystery?


It was on September 5th, 2006, the Tuesday following the Labor Day weekend, that Evergreen was launched into reality.8 Anyone out there familiar with library system migrations knows how exhausting, challenging, and demoralizing they can be. Let me make sure I drive this point home then. On launch day—after a purported sleep-deprived weekend for the PINES team—all two hundred and fifty-three libraries now in their care successfully went live with Evergreen.9


Library systems sat up and took note of this groundbreaking development and, today, there are more than two thousand libraries around the world that use the Evergreen library management system.10 Its users really care about their friendly, open-source software too. Evergreen, as befits the name, is a living, breathing community that vigorously responds to the careful and enthusiastic stewardship of its members who come together to write code, fix and report bugs, create documentation, test new versions of the software, and meet to share knowledge. Evergreen grows bigger and better every year.11


I started working with the PINES team in 2024 when Evergreen was really quite grown up. While it took me a minute to realize the significance of its development, it did not take me long to comprehend the passion that the PINES team feels, to this day, for their creation. While the initial developers had, due to conflict-of-interest considerations, left PINES to create their own support company in the very early days, that change had been born from legal necessity rather than from personal choice. It’s a bit cheesy, but I think the PINES staff, both past and present, should be really proud of their monumental achievement. By pretending it was magic they just about made that magic real.


Recently, I attended Evergreen’s twentieth birthday celebration. The event—replete with not one but two cakes—was held during the annual Evergreen conference. It goes without saying that I ate a slice of both. One had a citrus flavor, reminiscent of key lime pie. The other was more subtle, pink butter cream with delicate floral notes. I was excited to be at the shindig and a little smug about my excellent timing. I got to meet one of the original developers, and it felt a little like meeting a celebrity. I found myself strangely moved knowing that I was now part of this shared history. I’ve very much enjoyed my job as an Evergreen cataloger since the beginning, but I would now consider myself an enthusiastic advocate for all that our software stands for as well. Okay, it’s been a long speech. So, without further ado, let us raise a toast: Happy birthday, Evergreen. May your feet always remain on the road, may your encounters with dragons be few, and may your magic always endure.

item.title: Review of How to Study Public Life (Issue 1)
item.description:
Review of How to Study Public Life (2013) by Jan Gehl and Birgitte Svarre. Island Press, 200 pp., $40.

by J. Morgan Rowe-Morris

Publication details

Humanities Methods in Librarianship, Issue 1

Publication date: September 16, 2026

Author details

Affiliation: University of Texas, Arlington, TX, USA

ORCiD

Keywords

public life study; library assessment; third place; library buildings; libraries as place; public space; patron behavior; library theory; library design

For at least 20 years, librarians have been using third place theory to explain the importance of libraries to their communities.1 We have seized on Oldenburg and Brisset’s theory2 as a way of justifying and conceptualizing the important work that libraries do in their communities. This argument borrows from sociology and urbanism a vocabulary to talk about a concept that both librarians and their patrons knew intuitively. The library as place matters. This isn't a new concept, nor is the idea of a third place necessary to stress the importance of the library as a vital public space.3 The theory of the third place provides a useful conceptual framework and a formal language that extends beyond library science.


We see this concretely in the way our organizations describe themselves. My institution’s Campus Master Plan describes our central library thus: “The library is the second campus hub, alongside the University Center, where students gather for study, collaboration, creative pursuits, and relaxation.”4 The library is “a hub of learning, socializing, and creative work” and is “one of the most intensely used buildings on campus.”5 On my campus, the library is a vital center of public life and valued alongside other centers of campus life like the University Center. My former institution and our supporting stakeholders used similar language to describe our role as a large urban public library.6 My colleagues from school libraries use similar language to describe the role of their libraries in their learning community.


Despite this acknowledgement of the role of libraries in the public life of our varied communities and promotion of the library as a public space, the library literature has little to say about how librarians should evaluate libraries as public space, or what makes some libraries spaces better than others. We look at gate counts and computer usage but know relatively little about what our patrons do while they are in the library. Most library workers have an understanding of what works and what doesn’t in their spaces,7 but there is little way to formalize that knowledge or communicate it to the decision makers in our institutions.


Our disciplinary foundation is limited and often focused on assessing limited sets of library use like seating.8 Here, we can turn to other disciplines for help. While urban design is largely focused on the spaces between buildings, I would argue that the library as a public space is a suitable object for study using the urban design research method called public life study.


How to Study Public Life by Jan Gehl and Birgitte Svarre is intended to introduce urban designers to the use of direct observation in the assessment of public space. In contrast to the digital surveillance methods of smart city urbanism and algorithmic public management, public life study emphasizes the role of the trained observer in the process of understanding how people behave in public spaces and why they behave that way.9 It is an inherently human process that is about transforming observation into understanding.


This is a relatively short book and written in an approachable style that avoids unexplained jargon. The research notes chapter prevents brief case studies of different public life studies. The public life studies in practice looks at the life of a handful of studied cities after observation and intervention. The final chapter discusses the role of public life studies in policy formation. The question framework, tools and case studies are most likely to be useful to librarians. These sections of the book introduce, in general terms, a set of tools that can be readily adapted by librarians evaluating their spaces.


It isn’t hard to see how libraries could adapt the study looking at the effect of fear on traffic patterns in Copenhagen or the examination of how the number and placement of benches affects space use in Oslo. These are questions that impact our space every day. Likewise, the application of mapping, tracing and counting techniques to libraries seems intuitive.


This approach can begin to help us systematize our knowledge of our spaces as spaces. Serious uses of public life study will require additional work and reading,10 but as an introduction to a way that we can learn from our buildings11 and improve our spaces, it provides a productive starting point.


I believe an understanding of public life study can serve two important roles for librarians. It can help us to better understand the use of our spaces, and it can help us formalize and communicate the things we know about our libraries. In the first case, public life study lets us know our spaces in ways that go beyond our own preconceptions and fears. We can begin to answer the question of what spaces in our buildings are actually of use to our patrons,12 and to what use our patrons put the spaces that we have provided. In the second case, librarians and library workers know important things about our spaces and services.


Often, we understand through hard-earned experience important details about how our spaces function. If we can formalize and communicate that knowledge we can, perhaps, avoid repeating past mistakes and make our spaces more functional and inviting.


This book doesn’t do that alone—there is much work within the discipline that still needs to be done—but as a starting point for library workers interested in learning from their spaces and administrators interested in making better decisions about the library as a place for people, it serves admirably.

item.title: Review of Triptych: Death, AI, and Librarianship (Issue 1)
item.description:
Review of Triptych: Death, AI, and Librarianship (2025) by R. David Lankes, Jain Orr, and Qianzi Cao. Self-published, 89pp, $25.00

by Joel Blechinger

Publication details

Humanities Methods in Librarianship, Issue 1

Publication date: September 17, 2026

Author details

Affiliation: MacEwan University, Edmonton, AB, Canada

ORCiD

Keywords

artificial intelligence; vocational awe; loneliness epidemic; deprofessionalization

R. David Lankes, Jain Orr, and Qianzi Cao’s new book Triptych: Death, AI, and Librarianship is a wildly uneven text.1 Within any one of its sections—even across the span of several pages—Lankes may genuinely provoke the reader only to follow up a compelling insight with a nearly meaningless declarative statement. Though, as its title page asserts, Triptych is published “in association” with Library Journal, what this association amounts to is promotional muscle,2 and, regrettably, not editorial assistance. Lankes—Professor of Librarianship at the University of Texas at Austin’s iSchool and author of past titles from MIT Press, like 2011’s The Atlas of New Librarianship and 2016’s The New Librarianship Field Guide—elected to self-publish Triptych due to the urgency of the topics he covers.3 While working one’s way through the short text, one wishes that its author would have felt perhaps less urgency to meet the moment and more desire to shape and refine the book’s arguments.


Triptych consists of three related lectures: “From Serving to Saving,” “AI, Joy, and Social Connectedness,” and “Librarians and Their Feral Kin.” These sections are rounded out by a foreword, a brief introduction, a glossary (where Lankes attempts to clarify some of his key terminology), a short coda, and a separate “supplement” (“Librarians and the ‘Loneliness Epidemic’”) authored by Orr. The high-level arguments that Lankes makes in each lecture are relatively easy to gloss, though, in each section, he tends to indulge in confusing digressions that—had he not chosen to go the self-publishing route—a skilled editor likely could have reined in. “From Serving to Saving” is, as its title suggests, about how “we in librarianship must focus on saving lives” in response to “deaths of despair.”4 Along the way, Lankes digresses—with varying degrees of coherence—on the importance of narrative, the threat posed by the parental rights movement, the war currently being waged on libraries by American courts, abandoning neutrality for “professionalism,” how more librarians and teachers need to run for office, and, finally, he recounts a story about an extremely alienated Uber driver that served him in Springfield, Illinois.


“AI, Joy, and Social Connectedness” is, by far, the weakest of Lankes’ lectures, and, as a result, perhaps the hardest to try to summarize. As far as I have been able to piece together from combing through the section multiple times, essentially, Lankes’ argument is that libraries and librarians are facing a polycrisis comprised of “dark and hard topics,”5 including climate catastrophe, war, the decline of western democracies, book banning, social media-fueled disinformation and alienation, deaths of despair, and pandemics. In the face of this polycrisis, Lankes suggests that librarians must choose joy, and reinvest in their local communities, perhaps abandoning the rigidity of the universalizing and standardizing tendencies inherited from what he terms “the industrial library.”6 Due to generative artificial intelligence’s (GenAI’s) emergence and the public’s increased skepticism of all media, Lankes indicates that a new information literacy is also now required, and that librarians need to work to rebuild trust in their communities through movement building and storytelling. In ways that are not exactly specified, however, librarians also “need to experiment with and influence AI tools to ensure fairness and ethical standards”7 and “try AI in open sessions with the community.”8


Finally, Lankes’ last lecture, “Librarians and Their Feral Kin,” jumps off from his own experiences touring Dutch libraries, which—according to Lankes—are innovative and responsive to their communities’ needs despite the fact that the Netherlands ceased granting formal library degrees in the mid-1990s. This leads Lankes to consider whether library science degree programs in North America may be “instruments of inertia”9 and to argue for an expanded definition of “librarian” beyond formal degree-holding individuals. He urges the profession to embrace so-called “feral librarians”: “cadres of librarians who took alternative paths into the profession … [that] have been instrumental in forming a new librarianship, one of constant reinvention.”10 In one of the book’s most provocative stretches, Lankes entertains the possibility of the end of centralized, ALA-approved credentialing for library professionals in the United States, and analyzes what might in the future be a patchwork, state-based system. The assumption is that, with states like Texas working to remove the ALA-degree requirement from its definition of librarian, and other states like Georgia actively militating against the ALA, library programs should take this as an opportunity to reenvision library education and to extend an olive branch to those innovating in the profession that may not, strictly speaking, hold ALA-accredited master’s degrees.


While better written and certainly more focused than Lankes’ lectures, Orr’s supplemental essay feels tacked on to the volume, and her argument actually reads as if it contradicts some of Lankes’ earlier points from his first lecture about the urgent life-saving project of librarianship. Orr problematizes popular framings of the “loneliness epidemic,” suggesting that such views are illustrative of a moral panic that “obscures the deeper aspects of economic and social responsibility required to adequately address the issue [of loneliness].”11 Curiously, it is in Orr’s piece that capitalism receives its sole mention in the book, despite Lankes’ obsession with what one might term many of its morbid symptoms in the bulk of the text. Orr’s conclusion regarding libraries’ role in counteracting loneliness is much less ambitious than Lankes’ and definitely lacks his missionary zeal: “Whether we like it or not, libraries are already serving as social infrastructure to help people cope with loneliness. Instead, I believe that to the extent that libraries exist, they already do as much as can be done.”12 Orr is given the last word on the matter in Triptych via the placement of the essay, which is strange because it effectively qualifies—if not undermines—Lankes’ impassioned first lecture.


As other reviews of Triptych have identified,13 the book’s strength lies in Lankes’ bold approach to making his points, which could perhaps make it a worthwhile read to inform a larger group discussion in a book club or staff development day setting. For example, though Lankes is aware of Fobazi Ettarh’s concept of “vocational awe”14 and emphasizes that he “[is] also calling for supporting the library workforce”15 while proselytizing his salvific vision for libraries, spirited debate would likely ensue in any library workplace about how realizable a non-vocational awe-inspiring life-saving library raison d'être could even be. Similarly, Lankes’ call to embrace “feral librarians” is sure to ignite a powder keg of feelings around deprofessionalization, as was noted by Kuehn in his review.16 Where the book falls short repeatedly, however, is in Lankes’ aversion to offering many specifics, and this paucity of detail in his arguments will probably also limit useful discussion of his ideas due to his persistent lack of focus or clarity.


In addition to Lankes’ overtly stated views on AI explored in both his glossary and his second lecture, the reader of Triptych also has to navigate the GenAI content that he chooses to thread throughout the text. At the book’s outset, Lankes includes an AI disclaimer where he shares that the “conversation starters” at each section’s end have been created with Google’s NotebookLM, and that the book’s many images are products of Midjourney and ChatGPT. He is quick to emphasize his own oversight of the GenAI tools, his responsibility for their output, and even that his use of such tools “will be a deal breaker for a lot of people.”17 Lankes’ justification for using GenAI in Triptych is fairly standard: he views it as a tool that he needs to actively try out in order to comprehend it better, and that, ultimately, he “look[s] to engage in a conversation about AI, the mission of librarians, and its impact in society”18 that will, presumably, be brought about through his own GenAI use in the text. As evinced by Lankes’ release in February 2026 of an “AI free” version of Triptych, in his own words “a conversation was indeed had,”19 though I have not been able to corroborate where exactly this conversation may have taken place.


Overall, one wonders why Lankes’ GenAI experimentation necessarily had to make its way into the published work. It is puzzling that he manages to be simultaneously sensitive to the host of epistemological issues raised by the flood of GenAI content online and the consequent erosion of public trust (see lecture two), yet he then integrates GenAI images—even if disclaimed as such—so cavalierly into his own book. He is right to note—as he does in the blog post announcing the “AI free” edition—that Triptych’s GenAI elements, most markedly its images, “[introduce] a sort of fatigue when engaging the text.”20 In addition to fatigue, Lankes is also correct in identifying (in the same blog post) that the inclusion of the AI-generated images—along with a not insignificant number of typos and awkward phrasing errors—works to sow seeds of doubt in the reader regarding the book’s other elements that are ostensibly GenAI free.


For several years now, I have been fascinated to observe that the readerly experience is consistently, even programmatically, elided in contemporary AI discourse. Just as the brashest AI boosters only ever tend to imagine themselves as the dynamic human-in-the-loop leveraging agentic AI to automate tasks and never the workers whose quality of work has been severely degraded (if not whose jobs have been entirely eliminated by AI automation), the same figures rarely, if ever, acknowledge what it might feel like to interface with reams of AI-generated content. In our present world of automated summary and synthesis, perhaps the implicit expectation is that—in line with so-called “dead internet theory”21—no one will ever “read” generated text in a traditional sense, aside from other peoples’ agents who will then retrieve the “content,” serving it back to the user as part of a synthesis matrix or enhanced with now “helpful” executive summary-styled headers and bullet points. Though Lankes claims to not have used GenAI to write Triptych’s main text, his approach to using the technology to craft his “conversation starters” and to output a cache of—completely superfluous and deeply irritating—GenAI images exhibits a similar hostility to the act of reading that he seems to have only become aware of retrospectively and partially. As I have noted in a past review of a more generalist AI text, Ethan Mollick’s Co-Intelligence,22 works like Co-Intelligence (and now Triptych) can ultimately be read against the grain as symptoms of publishing in the AI age. My conclusion here is nearly identical to the one I reached after making my way through Mollick’s book: this is an age where having bold ideas without meaningful specifics to support them can seemingly get one farther and farther by the day, where book-like objects are rapidly replacing books, and where a fundamentally degraded experience of reading is itself becoming increasingly ordinary.

item.title: Review of Hayek’s Bastards: The Neoliberal Roots of the Populist Right (Issue 1)
item.description:
Review of Hayek's Bastards: The Neoliberal Roots of the Populist Right (2025) by Quinn Slobodian. Penguin, 279pp, $20.00

by Michael Kirby Hall

Publication details

Humanities Methods in Librarianship, Issue 1

Publication date: September 16, 2026

Author details

Affiliation: Kingsborough Community College, CUNY, Brooklyn, NY, USA

ORCiD

Keywords

authoritarianism; neoliberalism; neocolonialism; populism; F.A. Hayek

After ten years of right-wing triumph across the globe, but certainly after Trump’s abduction of Nicolás Maduro and the disastrous military campaign in Iran, political commentators across the spectrum have begun to ask: Is the “rules-based” international order dead? And, if so, have the stories it told itself about capitalism—its supposed “openness,” its “democratizing” influence—met a similar fate? Has the so-called neoliberal turn that began in the late ‘70s (and uniformly denounced by leftists) been clearing the way, in the end, for something much more insidious? These are some of the same questions that animate Quinn Slobodian’s recent book, Hayek’s Bastards: The Neoliberal Roots of the Populist Right.


As the title suggests, Slobodian partially focuses on the work of F.A. Hayek, an Austrian economist (tangentially) associated with what would come to be known as the Chicago School. Its members provided the theoretical foundations of neoliberalism (the primacy of the price mechanism, monetarism, etc.). Unlike his fellow Chicagoans, however, Hayek underpinned many of his claims about human nature with racist rhetoric; his insistence that free markets can only work in “civilized” nations was a thread that was eventually picked up by right-wing nationalists in the 21st century. Slobodian, therefore, offers a direct challenge to voices on both center-left and right who continue to insist that neoliberalism favors “free and open” markets and that, if given enough time, tends towards the realization of a post-racial world. Like many leftists before him, he entirely disputes the notion that globalized capitalism has led to uniform (racial, political, material) progress:

The right-wing neoliberals who joined, and in some cases founded, new populist parties did not reject the dynamic of market competition; they deepened it. ‘Closed borders’ libertarians continued to demand free movement for capital and goods; they simply drew a hard line against certain kinds of people.1

Capitalism’s global expansion has been, for the most part, a win for the Global North’s upper and middle classes but is itself reliant on various neocolonial structures (like the International Monetary Fund, inequitable trade deals, etc.). This is a familiar argument, but Slobodian is unique in his insistence that this racialized dynamic existed within neoliberalism since its inception; “free markets” for us (the Global North) and not them (the Global South) is, for him, a defining feature of the world post-globalization: “…we can see that important factions of the emerging Right were, in fact, mutant strains of neoliberalism. The parties dubbed as right-wing populist, from the United States to Britain and Austria, have rarely been avenging angels, sent to smite economic globalization.”2


These parties have instead met the challenges of globalization—the hollowing out of the industrial core, the collapse of the welfare state—with a lot of talk about fixing the problem via “reinvestment” in the metropole. But, as one can imagine, the right-wing parties in the Global North have put in little effort into addressing the negative effects of capitalist accumulation and, in most cases, have continued to support continued disinvestment along neoliberal lines (Elon Musk’s DOGE being one obvious example). One of the only things they have done, unsurprisingly, is double down on anti-immigrant rhetoric (as if immigrants were themselves the main drivers of globalization) while coextensively calling for a renewal of “national pride” and patriotism. Slobodian has a name for this agglomeration of discourses: “We could call it a language of Volk capital.”3


It is important to emphasize that this Volk capital is not just a return to Nazism or the fascism of wartime Italy. In addition, it is an explicit weaponization of hierarchies that existed prior to or are coextensive with formation of capitalism in its mercantile phase; one might think of it as a retread, in another sense, of extractive colonialism. But where the (neo)colonial underpinnings of neoliberalism were downplayed in its external rhetoric (the face it shared with the world), the rhetoric of Volk capital explicitly embraces the language of domination, of conquest and bloodshed.


This is all happening, of course, in a post-Soviet world, where the threat of “actually existing socialism” is long dead. Volk capital, in other words, does not set itself against socialism as it’s typically understood (as a political movement focused on the “purely economic.”) It is, rather, a form of capitalism that has somehow become even more paranoid in its victory, a capitalism that no longer sees socialism as a legitimate threat but continues to require an external enemy around which to organize itself: “This was a postmaterialist or nonmaterialist ideology… described as a mutant socialism. It traded in chromatic signs and skin tones; a socialism of pigmentation instead of redistributed wealth.”4


This turn away from the (supposedly) colorblind tenets of neoliberalism has been the focus of various other books in recent years. In his review of one such study, Arnaud Orain’s Le monde confisqué. Essai sur le capitalism de la finitude [The World Confiscated: An Essay on the Capitalism of Finitude], Nicholas Mulder sums up the defining features of what is called “finite capitalism”:

… first, the closure and monopolization of seas and oceans; second, the militarization of maritime commerce; third, the creation of anti-competitive organizations by capitalists; fourth, the carving up of markets and trade networks into politically exclusive silos; fifth, the usurpation of sovereign powers by mercantile interests; and sixth, the conversion of weaker and poorer parts of the Earth into subjugated resource empires for rich and powerful states.5

I bring up this specific example because I believe it works as a useful addendum to Hayek’s Bastards; we, along with Orain, might suggest that capitalism is better understood as the movement between two poles, between finitude and limitlessness, between disguised racism and unabashed racism. What we have called “neoliberalism,” in this reading, is not so much a stage in capitalism’s development but the movement of capital towards one pole in a specific historical moment. Volk capital or finite capitalism is the backwards swing of the pendulum.


Where is the academic library in all of this? We might begin by asking how best to defend library workers in an educational environment that is largely privatized but also increasingly policed by an illiberal government engaged, as Slobodian puts it, in a “zero-sum competition” in which any and all dissent must be crushed.6 Librarians, in other words, have the unfortunate task of continuing to fight neoliberalism at the level of the institution while simultaneously confronting Volk capital at the level of national politics. Sometimes, the latter provides convenient cover for the former’s continued drive toward total privatization.


To name just one prominent example, we have the case of Columbia University, which recently agreed to a whole host of Trump-imposed concessions that weaken the academic freedom rights of its faculty.7 With this tacit backing from the government, Columbia’s administration has felt emboldened to crackdown on dissent, effectively dismissing, in one instance, a tenured law professor for her support of pro-Palestinian causes.8 And while (at least to my knowledge) this has not yet affected Columbia’s librarians, one can easily imagine the various ways in which this playbook could be (and already has been) taken up by other universities—with especially disastrous results in areas of the country where academic freedom protections for librarians are substantially weaker than in New York. This is merely a positional statement (a brief one, at that), but in this historical moment of crisis, it is important to clarify the moments where our enemies—from both the authoritarian right and from the neoliberal center—might converge.


In this sense, Hayek’s Bastards is an invaluable tool; it is a timely reminder that “the aggressive right becomes a functional force both when the ruling class is relatively weak and resorts to extreme measures to defeat a revolutionary threat … and when the ruling class is strong and decides to finish the job.”9 This is how Columbia’s (and Texas A&M’s and the University of Oklahoma’s…) recent acquiescence to the Trump administration should be understood: collaboration between neoliberal administrators and authoritarians, both chomping at the bit to finish the job of killing higher education.
